guidance.summary:

- **Roseola (HHV-6):** fever × 3-5 days, then diffuse maculopapular rash as fever resolves. Benign.
- **Viral gastroenteritis:** fever, vomiting, diarrhea. Assess hydration status.

guidance.title: Parapharyngeal Abscess
guidance.summary:
**Definition:** Deep space neck infection involving the parapharyngeal (lateral pharyngeal) space — a fascially enclosed space extending from the skull base to the hyoid bone, lateral to the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle and medial to the pterygoid muscles, parotid gland, and mandible. Divided by the styloid process into two clinically significant compartments:

- **Prestyloid compartment:** Contains fat, lymph nodes, internal maxillary artery, inferior alveolar nerve. Most infections originate here (dental, pharyngeal, tonsillar source).
- **Poststyloid compartment (carotid sheath):** Contains internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, cranial nerves IX-XII, sympathetic chain. Infection here causes vascular complications (carotid erosion, IJV thrombosis) and cranial nerve palsies.

**Etiology:**
- Odontogenic (most common in adults — 30-50%): infected lower molars, periapical abscesses
- Pharyngeal/tonsillar: spread from peritonsillar abscess or pharyngitis
- Parotitis: direct extension from parotid space
- Iatrogenic: dental extraction, peritonsillar drainage, injection
- Penetrating trauma to neck or oral cavity
- IV drug use (injection into neck vessels)

**Microbiology:**
- Polymicrobial in 50-70%: Streptococcus (viridans group, GAS), anaerobes (Prevotella, Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium), Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA)
- Fusobacterium necrophorum: Lemierre syndrome pathogen — IJV septic thrombophlebitis

**Clinical Features:**
- Fever, rigors, toxic appearance
- Unilateral neck swelling and induration below the angle of mandible
- Odynophagia, dysphagia
- Trismus (less severe than PTA — pterygoid inflammation is less direct)
- "Hot potato" voice or muffled speech
- Torticollis (head tilted toward affected side)

guidance.title: Acute Epiglottitis
guidance.summary:
1. **Forcing the patient supine for examination or imaging.** Supine positioning collapses the already compromised airway. Examine and image with the patient sitting upright.

2. **Performing blind oropharyngeal exam with a tongue depressor.** Direct oropharyngeal manipulation triggers laryngospasm and complete airway obstruction. Use flexible nasopharyngoscopy in a controlled setting.

3. **Delaying ENT/anesthesia notification because the patient "looks stable."** Epiglottitis deteriorates unpredictably. Dual specialty notification (ENT + anesthesia) happens at time of suspicion, not after confirmation.

4. **Anchoring on the classic pediatric presentation in adults.** Adult epiglottitis presents with severe sore throat and dysphagia more than stridor and drooling. A severe sore throat with a relatively normal oropharyngeal exam demands further evaluation.

5. **Attempting ED intubation in a semi-stable patient.** OR intubation with fiber-optic guidance, ENT backup, and surgical airway readiness is the standard. ED intubation is reserved for complete airway loss.

6. **Discharging as "pharyngitis" without visualizing the epiglottis.** The oropharynx appears deceptively normal in epiglottitis — the pathology is supraglottic. Severe sore throat with pain out of proportion to exam findings warrants lateral neck X-ray or nasopharyngoscopy.

7. **Omitting MRSA coverage in critically ill patients.** Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus causes epiglottitis, particularly in immunocompromised patients and those with healthcare exposure. Add vancomycin in severe cases.

8. **Relying on a normal lateral neck X-ray to exclude epiglottitis.** Sensitivity is only 79-88%. A negative X-ray in a patient with high clinical suspicion requires direct visualization or CT.

Your throat is a tube that carries food to your esophagus and air to your windpipe and larynx. The technical name for your throat is the pharynx.

 Tonsillitis - inflammation of the tonsils 
 Cancer 
 Croup - inflammation, usually in small children, which causes a barking cough 
 Laryngitis - swelling of the voice box, which can cause a hoarse voice or loss of voice 
 

 Most throat problems are minor and go away on their own. Treatments, when needed, depend on the problem.

guidance.title: Adult Epiglottitis
guidance.summary:
**Classic presentation:**
- Severe sore throat disproportionate to pharyngeal findings
- Muffled "hot potato" voice
- Odynophagia, dysphagia, drooling
- Stridor (late finding — indicates critical narrowing)
- Tripod positioning (sitting upright, leaning forward, neck extended)
- Fever, toxic appearance

**Key exam findings:**
- Oropharynx may appear normal — epiglottis is below line of sight on routine exam
- Tender anterior neck, especially at hyoid level
- Cervical lymphadenopathy

**Common etiologies (adults):**
- Haemophilus influenzae (less common post-Hib vaccine era)
- Streptococcus spp. (pneumoniae, pyogenes) — now most common in adults
- Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA)
- Viral: HSV, parainfluenza
- Thermal/caustic injury, crack cocaine inhalation

**Red flags for imminent obstruction:**
- Stridor at rest
- Inability to swallow secretions
- Rapidly progressing symptoms (< 12 hours)
- SpO2 declining despite supplemental O2

guidance.title: Throat Cancer
guidance.summary:
Throat cancer is a type of head and neck cancer . Throat cancer has different names, depending on which part of the throat is affected. The different parts of your throat are called the oropharynx, the hypopharynx, the nasopharynx, and the larynx, or voice box. 

 The main risk factors for throat cancer are tobacco use and heavy drinking. Certain types of throat cancer also have other risk factors. For example, having HPV is a risk factor for oropharyngeal cancer. 

 Symptoms of throat cancer may include: 
 A sore throat that does not go away 
 A lump in the neck 
 Pain or ringing in the ears 
 Trouble swallowing 
 Ear pain 
 

 To diagnose throat cancers, doctors may do a physical exam and history, imaging tests, and a biopsy. You may also need other tests, depending on the type of cancer. Treatments include surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. Treatment for some types of throat cancer may also include targeted therapy. Targeted therapy uses drugs or other substances that attack specific cancer cells with less harm to normal cells. 

 NIH: National Cancer Institute

**Definition:** Deep space neck infection involving the parapharyngeal (lateral pharyngeal) space — a fascially enclosed space extending from the skull base to the hyoid bone, lateral to the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle and medial to the pterygoid muscles, parotid gland, and mandible. Divided by the styloid process into two clinically significant compartments:

- **Prestyloid compartment:** Contains fat, lymph nodes, internal maxillary artery, inferior alveolar nerve. Most infections originate here (dental, pharyngeal, tonsillar source).
- **Poststyloid compartment (carotid sheath):** Contains internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, cranial nerves IX-XII, sympathetic chain. Infection here causes vascular complications (carotid erosion, IJV thrombosis) and cranial nerve palsies.

**Etiology:**
- Odontogenic (most common in adults — 30-50%): infected lower molars, periapical abscesses
- Pharyngeal/tonsillar: spread from peritonsillar abscess or pharyngitis
- Parotitis: direct extension from parotid space
- Iatrogenic: dental extraction, peritonsillar drainage, injection
- Penetrating trauma to neck or oral cavity
- IV drug use (injection into neck vessels)

**Microbiology:**
- Polymicrobial in 50-70%: Streptococcus (viridans group, GAS), anaerobes (Prevotella, Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium), Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA)
- Fusobacterium necrophorum: Lemierre syndrome pathogen — IJV septic thrombophlebitis

**Clinical Features:**
- Fever, rigors, toxic appearance

Parapharyngeal Abscess
parapharyngeal space infection; lateral pharyngeal abscess; pharyngomaxillary space infection
Recognition
**Definition:** Deep space neck infection involving the parapharyngeal (lateral pharyngeal) space — a fascially enclosed space extending from the skull base to the hyoid bone, lateral to the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle and medial to the pterygoid muscles, parotid gland, and mandible. Divided by the styloid process into two clinically significant compartments:

- **Prestyloid compartment:** Contains fat, lymph nodes, internal maxillary artery, inferior alveolar nerve. Most infections originate here (dental, pharyngeal, tonsillar source).
- **Poststyloid compartment (carotid sheath):** Contains internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, cranial nerves IX-XII, sympathetic chain. Infection here causes vascular complications (carotid erosion, IJV thrombosis) and cranial nerve palsies.

**Etiology:**
- Odontogenic (most common in adults — 30-50%): infected lower molars, periapical abscesses
- Pharyngeal/tonsillar: spread from peritonsillar abscess or pharyngitis
- Parotitis: direct extension from parotid space
- Iatrogenic: dental extraction, peritonsillar drainage, injection
- Penetrating trauma to neck or oral cavity
- IV drug use (injection into neck vessels)

**Microbiology:**
- Polymicrobial in 50-70%: Streptococcus (viridans group, GAS), anaerobes (Prevotella, Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium), Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA)
- Fusobacterium necrophorum: Lemierre syndrome pathogen — IJV septic thrombophlebitis

**Clinical Features:**
- Fever, rigors, toxic appearance
- Unilateral neck swelling and induration below the angle of mandible
- Odynophagia, dysphagia
- Trismus (less severe than PTA — pterygoid inflammation is less direct)
- "Hot potato" voice or muffled speech
- Torticollis (head tilted toward affected side)

**Definition:** Rapidly progressive inflammation of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic structures, causing airway obstruction. Now predominantly an adult disease in the post-Hib vaccine era.

### Classic Presentation
- Severe sore throat disproportionate to pharyngeal findings
- Dysphagia, odynophagia, drooling
- Muffled "hot potato" voice
- Stridor (late and ominous — indicates >50% airway narrowing)
- Tripod positioning, neck extension ("sniffing position")
- Rapid onset (hours, not days)
- Fever, toxic appearance

### Adult vs Pediatric Differences
| Feature | Pediatric (rare post-vaccine) | Adult |
|---|---|---|
| Onset | Fulminant (hours) | Subacute possible (12-24 hours) |
| Drooling | Common | Less common |
| Airway obstruction | Rapid, higher risk | Variable, still dangerous |
| Etiology | H. influenzae type B (if unvaccinated) | Polymicrobial; Strep, Staph, H. influenzae non-typeable |
| Thumbprint sign | Classic | Present in 60-80% |

### Red Flags for Imminent Airway Loss
- Stridor at rest
- Inability to swallow secretions
- Sitting upright, refusing to lie down
- Cyanosis
- Altered mental status
- Rapid clinical deterioration
